lessons.title: Using materials: corrosion, alloys, ceramics and composites
lessons.summary: Find out why iron rusts and how to stop it, why alloys are stronger than pure metals, and how the properties of glass, ceramics, polymers and composites decide what they are used for.
objectives: I can explain what is needed for iron to rust and describe how rusting is prevented.
I can explain sacrificial protection in terms of reactivity.
I can explain why alloys are harder than pure metals and give the composition and uses of common alloys.
I can compare the properties of soda-lime glass, borosilicate glass, clay ceramics, polymers and composites.
I can explain how thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers differ in structure and behaviour.

activities.title: Rusting
activities.content:
## Why iron turns orange

**Corrosion** is the destruction of a material by chemical reactions with substances in its environment. The corrosion of iron is called **rusting**, and it is a big problem because so much of the world's infrastructure is made of steel.

### What is needed

Iron rusts only when **both water and oxygen** are present. A classic experiment uses three test tubes containing iron nails:

| Tube | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A | water and air | rusts |
| B | boiled water under a layer of oil (no oxygen) | no rust |
| C | air with calcium chloride to absorb moisture (no water) | no rust |

Remove either oxygen or water and rusting stops. Salt water speeds rusting up, which is why cars near the coast rust faster.

### The reaction

iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust)

Rust is soft and **flakes off**, exposing fresh iron underneath, so the corrosion keeps going until the object is eaten right through.

### Aluminium is different

Aluminium is more reactive than iron, but it does not corrode away. It reacts with oxygen to form a thin layer of **aluminium oxide** that sticks tightly to the surface and **stops any further reaction**. That protective layer is why aluminium is used for window frames and drinks cans.

activities.title: Preventing rust
activities.content:
## Two strategies

### 1. Keep out water and oxygen (barrier methods)

Coat the iron so that neither water nor oxygen can reach it:

- **Painting**: cheap, decorative, used on bridges and cars. Fails if the paint is scratched.
- **Oiling or greasing**: used on moving parts such as bike chains, because paint would crack.
- **Electroplating**: coating with a less reactive metal such as tin (food cans) or chromium (taps). Looks good and resists corrosion, but if the coating is scratched the iron beneath rusts faster.

### 2. Sacrificial protection

Attach a **more reactive metal** to the iron. Because it is more reactive, it **loses electrons more readily** and corrodes instead of the iron. It is sacrificed to protect the steel.

- Blocks of **zinc** or **magnesium** are bolted to ships' hulls and underground pipelines and replaced when used up.

### 3. Galvanising: both at once

**Galvanising** coats steel with a layer of **zinc**. The zinc acts as a **barrier** while it is intact, and if it gets scratched it also gives **sacrificial protection**, because zinc is more reactive than iron. This double action is why galvanised steel is used for gates, crash barriers and roofing.

### Alloying

**Stainless steel** contains chromium, which forms a protective oxide layer in the same way aluminium does, so it does not need any coating.

question.text: Why does a zinc block attached to a steel ship's hull stop the hull from rusting?
question.hint: Compare the reactivity of zinc and iron.
question.explanation: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it loses electrons and corrodes in preference to the iron. This is sacrificial protection.

options.text: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead of the iron.
Zinc keeps water away from the whole hull.
options.feedback: A single block cannot act as a barrier for the whole hull.

options.text: Zinc is less reactive than iron, so it draws oxygen away.
Zinc reacts with the salt in sea water to make it neutral.

question.text: Match each method of rust prevention to how it works.
question.hint: One is a barrier, one is a sacrifice, one is both.
question.explanation: Paint only keeps out water and oxygen; a magnesium block only corrodes in place of the iron; galvanising with zinc does both.

pairs.right: barrier that keeps out water and oxygen

activities.title: Alloys
activities.content:
## Why mixing metals makes them stronger

Pure metals are often too **soft** for practical use. In a pure metal the atoms are all the same size and are arranged in **neat layers** that can **slide** over each other easily, which is why pure gold or pure copper bends so readily.

An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. The added atoms are a **different size**, so they **disrupt the regular layers**. The layers can no longer slide easily, so the alloy is **harder** and **stronger**.

```
 pure metal          alloy
 o o o o o o         o o O o o o
 o o o o o o   →     o O o o o O
 o o o o o o         o o o O o o
 layers slide        layers jam
```

### Alloys you need to know

| Alloy | Made from | Useful because | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **bronze** | copper + tin | hard, resists corrosion | statues, bells, ship fittings |
| **brass** | copper + zinc | harder than copper, easy to shape | door handles, musical instruments, taps |
| **gold jewellery** | gold + silver, copper or zinc | harder than pure gold | rings; purity in **carats**, 24 carat = pure |
| **steel** | iron + carbon (+ other metals) | see below | almost everything |
| **aluminium alloys** | aluminium + magnesium, copper | low density but strong | aircraft, bicycles |

### Types of steel

- **High-carbon steel**: hard but **brittle**; used for cutting tools.
- **Low-carbon steel**: softer and easily shaped; used for car bodies.
- **Stainless steel**: iron with **chromium** and **nickel**; hard and **corrosion resistant**; cutlery, sinks.

### Gold carats

24 carat gold is 100% gold. 18 carat gold is 18/24 = 75% gold.

activities.title: Worked example: carat calculations
activities.content:
**A ring is made of 9 carat gold and has a mass of 6.0 g. What mass of gold does it contain?**

Carats are out of 24, so the fraction of gold is 9 ÷ 24 = 0.375.

Mass of gold = 0.375 × 6.0 = **2.25 g**

The other 3.75 g is silver, copper or zinc, which make the ring hard enough to wear every day.

**Why not use 24 carat gold?**

Pure gold is very **soft** because all its atoms are the same size and the layers slide easily. The alloying atoms are different sizes and disrupt the layers, making the metal much harder and more scratch resistant.

**Percentage purity from carats**

| Carat | % gold |
|---|---|
| 24 | 100 |
| 18 | 75 |
| 14 | 58.3 |
| 9 | 37.5 |

**The reverse:** an alloy is 60% gold. Its carat rating is 0.60 × 24 = **14.4 carat**.

question.text: A gold necklace is 18 carat and has a mass of 12 g. Calculate the mass of gold in the necklace in grams.
question.hint: 18 carat means 18 parts out of 24 are gold.

metadata.blanksText: In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers that can ___ over each other. In an alloy the added atoms are a different ___, which disrupts the layers and makes the alloy ___ than the pure metal.

question.hint: Think about what the layers do when a metal bends, and what the alloying atoms change.
question.explanation: Layers slide in a pure metal; different-sized atoms in an alloy stop the layers sliding, so the alloy is harder.

activities.title: Glass, ceramics and composites
activities.content:
## Materials that are not metals or plastics

### Glass

**Soda-lime glass** is made by heating a mixture of **sand** (silicon dioxide), **sodium carbonate** and **limestone**. It is cheap and used for windows and bottles, but it has a relatively low melting point.

**Borosilicate glass** is made from sand and **boron trioxide**. It has a much **higher melting point** and does not crack when heated suddenly, so it is used for laboratory glassware and ovenware.

### Clay ceramics

Pottery, bricks, tiles and china are made by **shaping wet clay** and then **heating it in a furnace** (firing). The heat causes chemical changes that lock the structure together. Ceramics are hard, strong in compression, heat resistant and unreactive, but **brittle**.

### Composites

A **composite** is made of two materials combined so that the properties of the whole are better than either part. There is always a **reinforcement** (fibres or fragments) embedded in a **matrix** (binder) that holds it together.

| Composite | Reinforcement | Matrix | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| fibreglass | glass fibres | polymer resin | boats, surfboards |
| carbon fibre | carbon fibres | polymer resin | racing bikes, aircraft parts |
| reinforced concrete | steel rods | concrete | bridges, buildings |
| plywood | wood layers | glue | furniture |

Concrete alone is strong in compression but cracks under tension; steel rods are strong in tension. Together they make a material that resists both, which is why reinforced concrete can span a bridge.

activities.title: Thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers
activities.content:
## Same monomer, different polymer

The properties of a polymer depend on **what it is made from** and the **conditions used to make it**. The classic example is poly(ethene):

- **Low density (LD) poly(ethene)** is made at very high pressure with a trace of oxygen. The chains are branched, so they pack loosely. It is flexible and used for carrier bags and cling film.
- **High density (HD) poly(ethene)** is made at lower temperature and pressure with a catalyst. The chains are straight and pack closely. It is stiffer and stronger, used for bottles and pipes.

Same monomer, different conditions, different product.

### Thermosoftening polymers

The polymer chains are **separate**, tangled together and held only by **weak intermolecular forces**. When heated, these forces are overcome, the chains slide apart and the polymer **melts**. It can be **remoulded** and recycled. Poly(ethene), PVC and poly(propene) are all thermosoftening.

### Thermosetting polymers

During manufacture, **strong covalent cross-links** form between the chains, joining them into one giant network. When heated, the cross-links hold firm, so the polymer **does not melt**. It stays rigid until it eventually chars. Thermosetting polymers are used where heat resistance matters: saucepan handles, electrical plugs and sockets, worktop laminates.

```
 thermosoftening        thermosetting
 ~~~~~~~   ~~~~~        ~~~~|~~~~|~~~~
   ~~~~~~~~~   ~~~          |    |
 ~~~~   ~~~~~~~~        ~~~~|~~~~|~~~~
 separate chains        cross-linked
```

question.text: Which statements about thermosetting polymers are correct? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about cross-links and what happens on heating.
question.explanation: Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links between chains, so they do not melt when heated; this makes them useful for heat-resistant items like plug casings. They cannot be remoulded by heating.

options.text: The chains are joined by strong covalent cross-links.
They do not melt when heated.
They can be melted and remoulded many times.
The chains are held together only by weak intermolecular forces.
options.feedback: That is the structure of a thermosoftening polymer.

question.text: Match each material to the property that makes it suitable for its use.
question.hint: Think about heat, weight and what each material is made of.
question.explanation: Borosilicate glass has a high melting point and resists thermal shock; carbon fibre composite is strong but light; bronze resists corrosion; thermosetting polymers do not melt.

pairs.right: high melting point, does not crack when heated

pairs.left: carbon fibre composite for a racing bike frame
pairs.right: very strong for its low mass

pairs.left: thermosetting polymer for a plug casing
pairs.right: does not soften when it gets warm

question.text:
A steel garden gate is coated with zinc.

(a) State the two substances that must both be present for the steel to rust.

(b) Explain two ways in which the zinc coating protects the steel, including what happens if the coating is scratched.

(c) The hinges are made of brass. Explain, in terms of structure, why brass is harder than pure copper.

(d) The gate handle is a thermosetting polymer. Explain why a thermosoftening polymer would be less suitable for a handle that gets hot in the sun.
question.hint: Water and oxygen. Barrier plus sacrificial. Atoms of different sizes. Cross-links versus weak forces.
question.explanation: (a) Oxygen (air) and water. (b) The zinc acts as a barrier stopping water and oxygen reaching the steel; if scratched, zinc is more reactive than iron so it corrodes in preference (sacrificial protection). (c) Brass contains zinc atoms of a different size from copper atoms, which disrupt the layers so they cannot slide over each other easily. (d) A thermosoftening polymer has only weak forces between chains and would soften or deform when hot, whereas the cross-linked thermosetting polymer keeps its shape.

markScheme.criterion: Zinc acts as a barrier keeping out water and oxygen
If scratched, zinc is more reactive than iron and corrodes instead (sacrificial protection)
Zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms
This disrupts the layers so they cannot slide over each other
Thermosoftening polymer has weak intermolecular forces and would soften/melt; thermosetting has cross-links and does not

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Rusting** needs both **oxygen and water**. Rust flakes off, so corrosion continues. Aluminium forms a protective oxide layer.
- Prevent rust with **barriers** (paint, oil, plating), **sacrificial protection** (zinc or magnesium, more reactive than iron), or **galvanising** (zinc: barrier and sacrificial).
- **Alloys** are harder than pure metals because atoms of **different sizes disrupt the layers** so they cannot slide. Bronze = Cu + Sn; brass = Cu + Zn; gold jewellery measured in **carats** (24 = pure); steels vary with carbon content; stainless steel contains chromium and nickel.
- **Soda-lime glass** (sand, sodium carbonate, limestone) is cheap; **borosilicate glass** (sand, boron trioxide) has a higher melting point.
- **Clay ceramics** are shaped wet and fired; hard but brittle.
- **Composites** = reinforcement + matrix: fibreglass, carbon fibre, reinforced concrete.
- **LD and HD poly(ethene)** come from the same monomer under different conditions.
- **Thermosoftening** polymers melt (weak forces between chains); **thermosetting** polymers do not (covalent cross-links).

practiceQuestions.hint: Two things are needed, not one.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Rusting needs both oxygen and water; in dry air there is no water, so iron does not rust.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Low density and high density poly(ethene) are both made from ethene. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The two forms are made under different reaction conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst) and have different properties; HDPE is stiffer and stronger. They are made from the same monomer, and both are thermosoftening.

options.text: They are made under different reaction conditions.
High density poly(ethene) is stiffer and stronger than low density poly(ethene).
They are made from different monomers.
High density poly(ethene) is a thermosetting polymer.

practiceQuestions.text: A bronze bell has a mass of 250 kg and is 88% copper by mass. The rest is tin. Calculate the mass of tin in the bell in kg.
Explain why aluminium does not corrode away even though it is more reactive than iron.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happens to the surface of the aluminium when it reacts with oxygen.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a thin layer of aluminium oxide on its surface. This layer sticks firmly to the metal and does not flake off, so it acts as a barrier that stops oxygen and water reaching the aluminium underneath. Rust, by contrast, flakes off and exposes fresh iron.

markScheme.criterion: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a layer of aluminium oxide
The layer is unreactive and sticks to the surface / does not flake off
It acts as a barrier preventing further reaction with oxygen and water

practiceQuestions.text:
A manufacturer is choosing a material for a saucepan handle. The options are a thermosoftening polymer, a thermosetting polymer and aluminium.

(a) Explain, in terms of structure, why the thermosetting polymer is the most suitable choice.

(b) Give one reason why aluminium would be a poor choice for the handle.

(c) Suggest one reason why the manufacturer might still choose a thermosoftening polymer for the lid knob, which stays cooler.
practiceQuestions.hint: Cross-links; conducting heat; recyclable and cheaper to mould.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The thermosetting polymer has strong covalent cross-links between its chains, so it does not soften or melt when the handle gets hot; a thermosoftening polymer has only weak intermolecular forces and would soften. (b) Aluminium conducts heat well, so the handle would get too hot to hold. (c) Thermosoftening polymers are cheaper and easier to mould, and can be recycled; since the knob does not get as hot, softening is not a problem.

markScheme.criterion: Thermosetting polymer has covalent cross-links between chains
So it does not melt / soften when heated (thermosoftening would soften because of weak intermolecular forces)
Aluminium is a good thermal conductor so the handle would get hot
Thermosoftening polymer is cheaper / easier to mould / recyclable
